utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, everyone. Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to deal with the issue of the demilitarisation of the enclaves. When you had discussions with members of the Dutch Parliament, you said that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had a special strategy in the enclaves and used them as a base to launch attacks on Serb positions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Attacks were launched out of the enclaves, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see, briefly, 1D3137 in e-court. Page 3 in e-court. Page 3 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to now look on the left side, the seventh or eighth line from the bottom. This was part of my thesis: [In English] "If you were a Bosnian, you could operate from the safe area of Srebrenica. You could conduct raids out of Srebrenica and so forth. To that extent, the UN was a shield, and the Bosnians were protected by the UN from the threats of the Serbian -- Bosnian Serbs doing anything about it."

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we -- I can't see the bottom, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The left column. Yes, now it's in the middle.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was your position; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think I'm explaining what I thought the Bosnian position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not trying to say you are justifying this. This is what you observed of the Muslim strategy; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Yes, that is what I observed and understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now look at the last paragraph: "If the UN were going to break out of this ..." Do you see that: [In English] "If the UN were going to break out of this, in my view, we had to fight. We had to demonstrate and show that we would fight, because if we did not, we would go on being a hostage of one and a shield of the other. From about mid-March --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's go up to the second -- go up, the top of the second row. Top row, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "From about mid-March, I was beginning to argue that we needed to understand the situation, and that if we were not going to make a difference, we were going to have to fight." [Interpretation] Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What strikes one immediately is that you had two choices. One is you waged war, and as experienced showed us, you waged war exclusively with the Serbs. And the second option was to demilitarise the enclave. Do you agree that those were the two choices?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. And this wasn't my decision, in the end. I was the commander on the spot, of course, and was developing my own view as to what the circumstances were, the situation that I was in. I think, if I recall correctly, what I'm saying, and I may even say it in that section, that I'm starting at that time to make recommendations to my commanders, Mr. Akashi and General Janvier, that the Security Council of the United Nations need to re-evaluate their situation or we would find ourselves in a fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Dutch parliamentarians clearly understood that it was the task of the UNPROFOR to make sure that the enclaves are demilitarised and populated by civilians, rather than being a base from which to launch attacks on Serb civilians.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, could I show you this same document at page 5 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is an introduction to the question I'm going to ask now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see that the Dutch parliamentarians consider that it's understood that an enclave is a demilitarised zone from which no attacks are launched?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the detail of the conversation with the Dutch parliamentarians, and it was -- the burden of the conversation, as I recall it, was to do with my saying to them that, You've got to take the caveats on the use of your forces away and then I might be able to use them, but at the moment I can't. I think I used the phrase, You'll need to give me a blank cheque.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that, but let us look now at page 5 to see how they understood this and what you replied. Mr. Koenders, the middle column --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the right-hand column. Could you please raise this page. It's at the bottom. We need to see the bottom of the page. Now we have it. Koenders says: [In English] "According to the mandate, these troops had to be disarmed. This was sort of an open-air prison, which could not be used for possible attacks outside Srebrenica or Zepa, which could invite certain actions by the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you agree with what Mr. Koenders said?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just reading it, one minute. I don't remember this bit of it. If we can read it all, I can probably recall some of it. But the -- I'd have to go back and look at the agreements that led to the safe areas to see whether there should have been an absolute disarming of people or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we ask the General to read his answers from the bottom to the next page. Let us know if you're done, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the bottom of this page to see what General Smith replied. No, lower the page and raise the cursor. Show the first half of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I need to go over the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Go down, yes. Next page. Did you read --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've got to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go back, please, and then we'll come back to this page. Perhaps here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go back to the previous page, the right-hand column, the upper part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is part of your answer: [In English] "What they did need to do, though, was to stop the Bosnians conducting operations from out of them. They needed to make sure that the UN acted to control the Bosnians and not let the Bosnians use the UN as a shield to their activities." [Interpretation] Did you find this part of your answer?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Yes, I've got it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this your position, and is it an answer to the question asked by Mr. Koenders?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We're having a conversation, and I am trying to explain -- the whole of that section is this explanation of what I call the "hostage and shield" situation, using Srebrenica as an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it clear from all of this that the Serb side was regularly attacked from the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that it's clear from that, but I -- you were attacked from the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. General Smith, in answer to the question from the accused which goes to the effect that, referring to Mr. Koenders' question: "According to the mandate, these troops had to be disarmed. This was sort of an open-air prison which could not be used ..." You didn't answer. But would you like to answer now, having read those portions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. They had not been disarmed. We were now in a different situation that I'd found myself in. The disarming had not occurred, and the circumstances have now moved on, and what I'm talking about here is the situation that I found myself in, not what might have occurred in a perfect world about 18 months before when the safe areas were established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that these attacks on the Serbian Army and Serb civilians, which is particularly important, the surrounding Serb villages, lasted for two years, and it was only after two years that the Serb Army decided to put a stop to this?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that the safe area had existed for about two years before it was -- it collapsed, it was attacked and collapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you agree that the Serb Army did not mount any campaigns to restrict these attacks for all of two years, it only defended itself passively?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak for the years that I wasn't there. But starting from sometime in March, I saw the Bosnian Serb Army conducting operations around Srebrenica, no doubt to defeat those attacks, but the sum of that was also the actions that I'd reported earlier in these -- in these proceedings on the convoys, and also there were attacks on OPs and so forth around the edge -- edges of the -- of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will come back to that, General. The fundamental issue is that the UNPROFOR did not disarm the 8th Tactical Group and later the 28th Division. They attacked us on a daily basis, and we defended ourselves passively, and we mounted an operation to stop this conduct only in the summer of 1995. Do you know of any Serb operation within those two years that would not qualify as passive defence?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in detail, but you -- there were certainly attacks on the external defences -- on the perimeter defences of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I could add, artillery attacks as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is our case that all those were counter-attacks and defence, and we will prove that. But is it the case that UNPROFOR did not fulfill its commitment to disarm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that is exactly the statement that you should refrain from making. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does the fact remain that UNPROFOR did not fulfill its commitment to demilitarise the enclave, and in that sense, as you put it, served as a shield for the Bosnian Army against us?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for sure that UNPROFOR had the duty to demilitarise -- disarm one of the sides. My recollection of the agreement, and it is only a recollection, is that it was the parties to the agreement, that is to say, yourselves and the Bosnians were to demilitarise. In this case, the Bosnians were to demilitarise. This was an agreement between the two warring parties. The business of the UN was to supply the Bosnians within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I call up in e-court -- or, rather, can this document be admitted, or, rather, one part of this interview in the Dutch Parliament? Or perhaps not. It's on the record. 65 ter 8631, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are tendering or not? No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not necessarily, if it's all on the record. 65 ter 8631.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just recalling the way the discussion went, my recollection is that the witness was encouraged to read a particular portion before responding, did so, and I don't think that part is on the record. So I tend to think that it's not a circumstance where something is read out and there's -- verbatim and in full, and then there's a response to that, but there are portions of this that were alluded to that aren't on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the Defence is not minded to tender and the Prosecution is minded to tender, we can admit it as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine. Just the relevant portions, of course, Your Honour, but I think otherwise the record is unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The 16 pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I don't mind the whole thing, but I was anticipating the pages that were the subject of the discussion in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But can we identify the pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We certainly can admit it in its entirety, if you want. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit the 16 pages as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2290, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's see 65 ter 8631. Can we now see page 2, or perhaps let the General see the entire page. Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First look at this passage that begins with: "At a meeting ..." This is the cover page, 18 April. This is addressed to Kofi Annan, for the information of General Wahlgren, and also sent to Wahlgren from Sarajevo. Now, page 2, please: "At a meeting held at Sarajevo on 17 April 1993, Lieutenant-General Mladic and General Halilovic, in the presence of Lieutenant-General Wahlgren, representing UNPROFOR, acting as a mediator, agreed the following:" Now let's look at paragraph 4. And the whole document, of course, is available: [In English] "The demilitarisation of Srebrenica will be complete within 72 hours of the arrival of the UNPROFOR company in Srebrenica. All weapons, ammunition, mines, explosives and combat supplies (except medicines) inside Srebrenica will be submitted /handed over to UNPROFOR under the supervision of three officers from each side with control carried out by UNPROFOR. No armed persons or units except UNPROFOR will remain within the city once the demilitarisation process is complete. Responsibility for the demilitarisation process remains with UNPROFOR." [Interpretation] This was the mediation of General Wahlgren, obviously drafted by his team, signed by Halilovic and Mladic and by the mediator, General Wahlgren. Is it clear from this document that it was agreed that the responsibility for the demilitarisation of Srebrenica rest with the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says is the demilitarisation process remains with UNPROFOR. The process isn't the result. And further up, it's agreeing that the explosives, mines -- sorry, weapons, ammunition, mines, explosives, combat supplies, et cetera, inside Srebrenica will be submitted or handed over to UNPROFOR, under supervision and with the control carried out by UNPROFOR. The submitting of it is the act of the party who holds the weapon, not UNPROFOR, as I read that. And I'm reinforced in that view by the line right at the top which says that this is an agreement between Mladic, and I can't remember the other name, and mediated. He's not making the agreement; he's mediating. Wahlgren, I mean. So this is an agreement between the two parties that UNPROFOR will be responsible for the process. They're both agreeing that UNPROFOR will do that, as I understand that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I understand that the third party who created this agreement and signed it also accepted it, because General Wahlgren never made any reservations in the document that it would not be the responsibility of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't said that UNPROFOR isn't responsible for something. What he signed for is to be responsible for this process.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we saw another agreement. So this is a second agreement. Thank you. Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1028, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was referring to D135. Yes, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 135, that's correct. Can we briefly see again D135, the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This agreement was confirmed by the two parties on the 8th of May. So 1D135. That's what I'm referring to. On the 8th of May, 1993, that's a bilateral agreement that both these parties confirm, but obviously it was also mediated by a third party: [In English] "... reaffirming the demilitarisation of the city of Srebrenica, have agreed on the following:" [Interpretation] Could we now just scroll down a little bit. A little further, please. This is good: [In English] "Any military operations is strictly forbidden (Article 60, Protocol 1, Additional to the Geneva Conventions)." [Interpretation] Could we now see the next page of this document, please, page 2. Article 5, the first paragraph: [In English] "UNPROFOR shall control the demilitarised zone." [Interpretation] So it doesn't say "would," it says "shall." That's quite specific. And then in this same paragraph, it goes on to say: "Non-combatants who are in or who are willing to enter the demilitarised zone, except members of UNPROFOR ..." [In English] "... are not permitted to have in their possession any weapon, ammunition or explosives. Weapons, ammunition and explosives in their possession shall be seized by UNPROFOR. "Combatants will not be allowed to enter or to be in the demilitarised zone." [Interpretation] This was signed by two parties. And then it says there that all arms will be seized by UNPROFOR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That this agreement was not just a local agreement, but, rather, a UN agreement, as it were, is something that you, yourself, also confirm in your book; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember confirming that in that -- I haven't seen, that I remember, this particular document for a very long time. You need to show me the pages in the book where I confirm that it is not local, but I can see from the top that it was done within the presence of the force -- the UNPROFOR commander. "Morillon," wasn't it, at the top of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could we please pull up 1D3196. That's your book. 1D3196. Let us see whether this concept of demilitarisation, where reference is made to Article 60 of the Protocol 1 of the Geneva Conventions, that this portion of the demilitarisation was, in fact, within the UN ambit, as it were. Can we see page 143 in the book, itself, please. In e-court, page 7. And the book, itself, that's page 341, at the very bottom of the page. 341: [In English] "The idea of having a zone ..." [Interpretation] Well, here in this paragraph, let me just find that spot: [In English] "Nonetheless, during the negotiations, the idea of demilitarisation, demilitarising the area around Srebrenica, was introduced by General Morillon, and the proposal began to be discussed again in capital cities and at the UN. In itself, this three-cornered dialogue - which became four-cornered once the overall UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb was included - reflects the immense complexity ...," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] Is it clear from this that the UN were actually the ones who proposed demilitarisation, we agreed to it, two agreements were signed, and they were binding on both sides or both parties, whereas the first one was specifically binding on the UN as well, and it is with these caveats that we actually stopped our actions against Srebrenica in 1993 and agreed to the provisions of this agreement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me start at the beginning of this question, or near the beginning. Which is the first one that you refer to? I'm not quite sure what that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first one was the agreement that was mediated by Wahlgren, where the two parties met and agreed and signed the agreement, which also specifies the UN obligation.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I agree with you that the idea of demilitarisation originates from, if not the UN, the nations in the UN, and it is being discussed in the UN and by those UN commanders, of which Morillon was the one on the ground. And we have two agreements being signed, one and April and the other in May, and I don't recall -- the one I remember reading and so forth is the one you've just shown me, the one Morillon is listed at the top. I don't remember having seen the Wahlgren one, and I can only assume that the understanding was at the time that the first one was a precursor to the second one, and that the two -- we must understand the two as the beginning and end of a process of creating this agreement, rather than as the -- entirely separate events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But as you say, I believe, in your book, you cannot be just a little pregnant. UNPROFOR did accept and agree that that would be its responsibility, and we then agreed to that, and we ceased -- I ceased all operations around Srebrenica in 1993, and we accepted an agreement that UNPROFOR actually reneged on. Now, were the consequences of the violations of those agreements, in fact, the basis for many of the misunderstandings that would ensue between the Serb side and the UN?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is clearly misunderstanding, if one cares to classify it in -- under that heading, throughout this story. If I could go back to the Morillon agreement, please, and see the section that you showed me again with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Exhibit D1028. No, I'm sorry, it's D135.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Perhaps the General can actually tell us what to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the first page, on the 8th of May, following the agreement that was mediated by General Wahlgren.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go on one more page. I think -- I can't remember the article number that you showed me, but it's the one that is about the -- Article 5, is it? Yes, thank you. Yeah. The -- I wasn't in command. I'm sitting in London when this is going on. My understanding of the interpretation -- the UN understanding of both this document and the preceding one was that the -- this was an agreement between the two parties, the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnians. The UN had mediated it, facilitated it, call it what you wish, and would, provided the two parties did what they'd agreed to, control, be responsible for the process, or whatever. That's my understanding of how this document was understood in the United Nations at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Not only did they mediate, General, but two UN generals signed off on this. And to us, this was a clear signal that there would be no armed men there, other than UNPROFOR troops. Is it clear from this, General, that these areas were, in fact, not demilitarised and that that was the source of the misunderstandings that we had with UNPROFOR, both in terms of the convoys and the positions of the enclaves, and all the other problems that had to do with the areas -- demilitarised areas? Now, first of all, do you know that the Secretary-General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my first question was:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does the General know of this description of the safe areas in Bosnia that was provided by the Secretary-General of the UN and the Security Council, that the safe areas actually had become strongholds of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him saying such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And, secondly, would you agree that this is the moment when our problems with UNPROFOR begin, in terms of the content and frequency of the convoys, which then also resulted in the bombing of the Serb positions and an exacerbation of the relations between the Serb side and UNPROFOR, which came as a result of the fact that the safe areas, the protected areas of Srebrenica and Gorazde, were not, in fact, demilitarised and that attacks were launched at us from those areas, and UNPROFOR wanted us to behave differently? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR wanted you to allow it freedom of movement to supply the humanitarian aid into the enclaves. That was what we were required to do at that stage. And, yes, from the moment we started the safe areas, there was, if you care to call it that, difficulties between us, UNPROFOR and the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will revisit the issue of the convoys later on. Now, my question is: Was it cheaper, more humane, and more just had UNPROFOR demilitarised those zones rather than using force against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you wanting me to make this judgement with hindsight or trying to put myself in the position at the time, because I can't really do either. I don't have enough information to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, what is your position today? Had the demilitarised areas -- had the safe areas been demilitarised, wouldn't that have been far more efficient than the action that had actually transpired which later on brought on the crisis?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure efficiency enters into this, but I find it impossible to answer that sort of question. It's entirely hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what it was that prevented your forces from demilitarising the enclave or, rather, disarming the units that were within the areas of the safe areas? So what was it that prevented you from disarming the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about when I'm in command? Because I can't answer for the -- my predecessors, and I certainly can't answer for the period when this -- in 1993, when this document is drawn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, what prevented you, during your tenure there, from demilitarising the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was very nearly two years of -- since these agreements had been made, and I was in no position to wind the clock back to 1993 and to start again. I could only begin where we were, and the enclaves had not been demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us now see what the true reason was for UNPROFOR's tolerance for the army of the Muslims in the enclaves. Could we see 1D137 again, although I believe that this document has already been tendered and admitted. That's P2290. In e-court, that would be on page 6. Could we see the left column on the top, the very beginning, beginning with: "Secondly ..." [In English] "Secondly, there were considerable other pressures to arm the Bosnians and to encourage them, from the United States and others. All of us faced another set of pressures, me, Zagreb, the Security Council or whatever. The Serbs demanded that we should police the other side in this agreement. That was precisely how the Bosnian Serbs were approaching the UN. You, UN, have agreed to this, and you agreed that they would be disarmed. Why do you not disarm them?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What pressures are you referring to here, and was this -- well, first of all, let me put this question: Was the Serb position clear, and did it derive from the agreement, in fact?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb position was quite clear. You wanted those enclaves -- you did not want any attacks to come out of those enclaves. You wanted them demilitarised. But the document you're showing me again, and the paragraph in question, I repeat, it's an explanation of what I have called previously the "hostage and shield" situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From your reply here, we see that you clearly understood that the US and others actually encouraged the Muslims, and there were pressures to arm them and to further encourage them; is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that the reason for the failure to disarm them in the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you, I cannot explain in that detail the situation in 1993, and the argumentation, if you like, that was going on at that stage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's take a look now at page 9 of this same document. Or, rather, my apologies, I'm referring to the other document, your book, 1D3196. 1D3196, and then page 9 in e-court. Otherwise, it's page 344 of the book, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to refer to the last paragraph: "If 'something must be done' became the main approach to the Balkan crisis ..." [In English] "... it was further complicated by the 'something' being the desire to use air power which emanated from the US. Washington was increasingly involved in the debate as to what to do about the Balkans, not least due to the powerful lobby by the Bosniaks and Croats." [Interpretation] Therefore, it would seem that you were fully aware that both the Muslims and the Croats, through the -- via Washington and the United States, actually exerted pressure on their enemy in the Balkan theatre?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of their influence, yes. At exactly what stage I became aware of it, I'm not sure, and I don't think it was as early as 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware of the NATO plans? Did you have insight into the NATO plans, General? And they have different names.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, NATO plans for the use of force in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that -- of one plan, in its absolute outline, and that was the one that was executed in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will return to the issue of the London Conference and the plans later on. Now, let us move on to the topic of the convoys, General. The misunderstandings surrounding this issue actually arose as a result of the fact that the protected areas were militarised and were used as a basis to launch attacks against the Serb side. We've agreed on that. Now, did you know that it was not in the Muslim interest for the convoys to actually reach the enclaves, and that it suited them to prevent the supplies from reaching their own population?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, before you answer, could we please admit this into evidence, this page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll add page 344 as well as 341, which we saw previously, to the existing exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You knew, General, didn't you, that it was in the interest of the Muslim army for the convoys not to reach where they should and that their people should actually be deprived of the aid and supplies?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that, no. I know of cases where -- particularly in the early stages of the safe areas, where the Bosnian Government did not want to have their people moved out of the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Speaking of that, can you recall that your predecessor, General Morillon, and all other commanders were under great pressure from the local population to allow them to leave?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're probably referring to the same case. This was in the early stages of the establishment of the Srebrenica safe area. And if I remember correctly, the -- a convoy of refugees were taken from Srebrenica, I think, towards Tuzla. After that, General Mladic would only allow empty vehicles to come to Srebrenica. And at that point, the Bosnian Government said that they didn't want anybody -- any of the population to be evacuated. This is occurring, I think, in this April period of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But referring to the first topic, the preventing and sabotaging the supplies of humanitarian aid, let us take a look at what you have to say in your book on page 340, the same document, 1D3196. Page 7 in e-court, please. On the left: "As the UNHCR official explained to Lord Owen ..." [In English] "... the Muslim pockets were used by the Bosniak Sarajevo government in November(1992) as pressure points on the international community for further action. The longer the aid convoys were unable to reach them, the greater the pressure on the mandate. When convoys did succeed, calls for firmer action were unwarranted. Two weeks after the first successful delivery, Muslims (Bosniaks) launched an offensive towards Bratunac (a Serb-held town just outside the besieged Srebrenica). Thus the integrity of UNHCR and UNPROFOR was undermined, further convoys were impossible, and the pressure for firmer action resumed." [Interpretation] And in your statement, page 14, the consolidated statement, paragraph 57 -- if you could take a look at your statement, page 14, paragraph 57, you say: [In English] "Mladic said that these concerns about the Bosnian Army's intention had led him to restrict the amount of food, medicine and food for the enclaves. He claimed that the United Nations was supplying the Bosnian Army. I replied that any attack on the UN safe areas would be condemned by the international community and would risk a response by NATO using air power against the Bosnian Serbs. This brought forward a tirade of threats of counter-action from Mladic." [Interpretation] So you were aware - and so was Lord Owen, only he was dealing with it only until the end of 1993 - you were aware of this position and the intentions of the Bosnian Government that they didn't really want these enclaves to be supplied by the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that correct? Yes, that's a question. It says, in your book, that you were aware of this manoeuvring by the Bosnian Government and their tricks. Mladic informed you about this, and he informed you about that as a legitimate concern for him, as a commander?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have shown me two documents. The first, the book, my book, there is a quote within the book. I don't think I'd read that quote or found that quote until the book was being written, so I can't say that I knew that, as stated in the book, right back in 1993. The -- undoubtedly, the point that is made in the book, that quote, was going on, but that isn't -- what is being explained there is, again -- and the reason the quote is there is to try and explain this "hostage and shield" situation in which I found the UN and myself was in. The Bosnians did want their people fed, but they were using their people to apply pressure in these circumstances. The remarks in my amalgamated statement at paragraph 57 are of 1995, some two years later, and there I am making the point that my business is the delivery of humanitarian aid, and by now, for the UN, also the safe area policy, and the -- and that was my duty and my concern at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But let us see from the Serbian point of view. Arms, ammunition, war material is arriving in the enclaves, enabling them to mount attacks from the enclaves on the Serbian Army and Serb civilians. Were you aware that the Bosnian Army in the enclaves was arming itself instead of disarming?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that arms were reaching them, but it was not the -- the UN were not knowingly delivering weapons and so forth to any party to this conflict, and certainly not into the enclaves. We were delivering the humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Has that page been admitted, page 340 of the book? Could it be added to the same exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I heard it was already added yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D3150 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Between being a hostage and being a shield, you opted not for being a shield, but helping that shield attack the Serbian side? I don't mean you, personally, although you did order the bombing campaign, but I mean the United Nations and the international community. It's not in the document. It's a question while we are waiting for the document. Between being a hostage and being a shield, you did not want to be a shield, but instead attacked the Serbian side; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't want to be in the "hostage and shield" situation, but I didn't need to attack the Serbian side. That was created in reaction to what occurred, or that decision was put in front of me in the reaction to what had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you just strengthened your function as a shield?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I continued to strengthen my function, as the UNPROFOR commander, to conduct what I'd been sent to do, which was to deliver the humanitarian aid and oversee the safe areas regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at this order that has to do with prevention of thefts of fuel and other supplies of UNPROFOR. It's dated 12 May 1995. It says: "We have reliable information that members of UNPROFOR, UNHCR and other international organisations have been transporting fuel illegally to Muslims in the enclaves of Sarajevo, Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica. "They smuggle fuel in double or large tanks on combat and non-combat vehicles, which they empty in the enclaves, leaving just the quantity needed for their return journey from the enclaves ..." Et cetera, et cetera. Now, please look at point 4 in the order. Can we scroll down, please: "Confiscate the surplus of fuel from large tanks, leaving just the quantity needed for their journey to the enclave and back to the check-point. On their return from the enclave, return the fuel against a receipt for quantities confiscated and/or returned." And the last point, 6: "Battalion commanders shall be responsible for the implementation of this order; they will make sure it is being implemented correctly and prevent any abuse." Do you see, General, that our army clearly understood that the Muslim army in the enclaves could not possibly be supplied with fuel by any other means than international convoys and UNPROFOR vehicles going back and forth?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that from that document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1029, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's our theory, and you like theories, General - that's good - that civilians received sufficient quantities of what they needed, whereas the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina abused that, grabbed the food for itself, and that again was abused and manipulated by black-marketeers and other criminals. Did you have any information about that? And can we see 65 ter 22794. Did you know about that, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I'm sorry, I thought you wanted me to look at another -- another document. Do you want me to look at another document or do you want me to answer the question before I see the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please first answer the question. Were you aware that there were abuses of humanitarian aid, and that was why we had the misunderstanding that we had?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this necessarily leads to the misunderstanding, as you call it, but, yes, there were abuses. There was at least one case in my time in command when a convoy was found to have some ammunition hidden in its -- in one of the pallets, if I recall correctly, and the -- the exact -- how the humanitarian aid was distributed and controlled on the inside of the enclaves was something that I had little oversight of because of -- it was handed to the Bosnian authorities inside the enclave. So I can't say that it was handled absolutely correctly, because I and my subordinates, military subordinates, did not have an oversight of those -- of those actions by the Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before we move to this document, would you please look at your statement again, paragraph 46 and paragraph 47. Would all the parties kindly look at the same. It has to do with your visit to Srebrenica and supplies. You say that there were two -- there was at least one, if not two, supply vehicles: [In English] "My aim in visiting Srebrenica was to visit the Dutch UN battalion to get the first-hand view of the situation in the enclave." [Interpretation] So you did get an insight into the situation in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, let's go back to that document, 65 ter 2274. Sorry, 22794. Just to identify the first page: "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of the Interior, State Security Service, SDB Sector Tuzla, State Secret." It's a report dated 12 January 1996: "Please find enclosed an overview of the available information on murders, criminal acts, prostitution, and similar in the area of Srebrenica during the period leading up to the occupation of this safe area." Now, in English we need page 6. Page 6 in English. The paragraph begins with: "In addition ..." "In addition to what has been said so far, in our conversations with refugees from Srebrenica, we also recorded information on a number of crimes committed by members of the 28th Division and certain leaders of the municipal organs of Srebrenica. These certainly contributed to the destabilisation of the overall situation and affected the security of this enclave. These criminal activities involved persons close to the aforementioned categories, and they constituted one of the links in the chain of the sale of humanitarian aid and oil on the black market, the illegal sale of weapons and so on." A key role was played by the commanding officers of the 28th Division, and so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you arrived, were you briefed about this aspect of the situation in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I knew that Naser Oric was the commander in that area, or was believed to be the commander in that area, but I wasn't briefed of the sort of things that are being alleged there in the paragraph beginning: "In addition to ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But it appears from this paragraph, and this was written by the Muslim police, that there is enough food, fuel and weapons to go around, and even enough for black-marketeering?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That doesn't imply that there's enough to go all around everywhere.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 7 in English. It says: "Out of humanitarian aid --" We have to find that paragraph: "In September 1994, Oric --" That's right: "Naser Oric and Mujo Mandzic were co-owners of three cafe bars in Srebrenica, which were in business up to the occupation of Srebrenica. Provisions for the cafe were purchased from Chetniks on the Yellow Bridge. "Quite a large quantity of goods from humanitarian aid was set aside for the 28th Division. A lot of these were sold on the market by Hamdija Fejzic, Suljo Konakovic ...," et cetera. Let's move on to page 8. There's another paragraph I want to look at before I ask a question. Paragraph 2: "Suljo Hasanovic, former chief of the Srebrenica National Defence Secretariat. "According to some information, Hasanovic took food and groceries from the humanitarian aid warehouse, sold a part of that on the market with the help of unidentified persons ..." And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that humanitarian aid was abused by being given to the army, our enemies, who should not have been present there in the first place, but also by being sold in the market?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're showing me is a list of -- that a policeman is reporting of various things that people have stated. I don't think anything is proved there. Whether it happened or not, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, General, this is an official report from the state police. They are reporting on the information they received, they got from their sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the General has given his answer. Don't argue with the witness, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 9 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We won't read it all. Just look at paragraph 5: "Dr. Avdo Hasanovic, chief of the war hospital in Srebrenica. "Medicines from hospital supplies were sold at prices of 100 to 200 German marks, which caused a large number of deaths, mostly among the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina troops." And then further down the page: "Enver Stitkovac. "Approximately 150 persons from Srebrenica came to Zepa and bought 1.150 litres of oil from Stitkovac at 1 Deutschmark a litre, and they sold this oil -- they resold it at 7 to 8 Deutschmark per litre. Stitkovac had purchased this oil from the members of the Ukrainian Battalion." Did you have any information, General, of this illegal trade in medical supplies and oil, fuel?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And, again, this is source reporting, I see no corroboration, and the Ukrainian Battalion wasn't in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is about Zepa. He went to Zepa to buy from the Ukrainians. But look at the next paragraph --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What, and then carried it back to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They resold it at seven times the price in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but what you're telling me, then, is that he was also able to travel with fuel from Zepa to Srebrenica through Serb lines. This may have been possible, but I'm -- it is why I -- I can only read what you're showing to me, but I don't know anything about it and I'm doubting its value.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, we will come to the border between Zepa and Srebrenica. They were illegally linked by an illegal action of the 28th Division, and that was one more reason why we wanted to separate them and clear a passage. But look at paragraph 7. From a humanitarian aid warehouse, members of the Command Staff of the 28th Division were able to take large quantities of goods: "Tursunovic did not need anybody's permission to enter the warehouse. Whenever he came, goods were issued to him, regardless of what or how much he wanted." And the last paragraph, can we scroll down: "Hakija Meholjic --" We can skip that bit. In Srebrenica, Meholjic had a stud farm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the General has given his answer as to the value of this document more than -- a couple of times. Reading out from this document is of no point. Now it's time to put your case and to move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any basis to admit this document through General Smith.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, General Smith confirmed that he knew there was smuggling and there was black-marketeering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's in evidence. That's not the basis to admit this document, specifically, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we would like to play some video-clips, and I'm looking at the clock, Your Excellency, could we take the break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Is there anything outstanding for admission from the previous documents? Has the page 340 of the book been admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be added.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in the Popovic et al trial, you saw certain videos and provided your comments on them. Could we now see 1D3227.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The check-point in Ilidza, and the trucks of the United Nations which had papers that they were carrying humanitarian aid for Muslims, the Serb Army discovered 24.500 rounds of ammunition. Today in Ilidza, a convoy was stopped carrying, from the airport, humanitarian aid for Butmir and Hrasnica. A routine control by the military police from Ilidza showed that containers containing flour have a double bottom, a hidden double bottom, and contain tin cases. That was sufficient reason to doubt the regularity of this convoy. "Members of the French Battalion, who were escorting the convoy, were unable to tell us what was in the bunkers underneath the containers. The convoy was stopped, and members of UNPROFOR and UNHCR and police were invited and the on-site investigation was carried out in their presence. Containers were removed from the truck and a crane separated the upper part of the containers from the platform to which it was fixed. "Journalist: Mr. Popovic, the investigation on-site has been completed. Tell us what you found in the trucks carrying humanitarian aid to Hrasnica. "Mr. Popovic: In the trucks, there were 12.7 ammunition rounds, 5.000 pieces, 7.9 sniper ammunition, 19.540 pieces. They were found, as you could see yourselves, in the hidden bottom below the container. This is the second time in our zone of responsibility of the Ilidza Brigade that we are finding weapons and ammunition inside humanitarian aid shipments. "Journalist: Did you see whose ammunition that was? Is that known? Where does it come from? "Mr. Popovic: All the ammunition was manufactured in Konjic and brought by air to the airport in Sarajevo, and after that by land, this time carried by French forces and escorted by them. "From the competent authorities of the UN, we required official information, but we were unable to get it. Instead, it was explained they had no authorisation to provide such info. Unofficially, a representative of the UNHCR claimed they had nothing to do with the trucks and the containers, and that their authority is exclusively over the cargo carried inside the containers. What was below the containers is none of their concern. "Representatives of the foreign legion apologised, saying they were only escorting the convoy, and the UN police claimed that they would investigate the case and inform us in due course. "Who up-loaded cargo on these trucks at the airport and where the ammunition was up-loaded is currently unknown to us. "What happens with -- what is happening with checks at the airport and how many such convoys have already passed, we don't know, but it is an indisputable fact that UNPROFOR is being exposed, for the umpteenth time, as carrying weapons and ammunition for Muslims under the guise of humanitarian aid."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the Popovic et al trial, your comment on your video is on page 17683 [Realtime transcript read in error "87863"], but we have it as 1D3204 in e-court. That's the transcript of your comments. 1D3204. It says here -- the page in e-court is 223. It's not the right page. The right page is 223 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the hard copy page would be what? It's not in the 87 range, so that was a misstatement. If we just get the right --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 17683 is the page number. That's the number we see at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you say here, General: [In English] "The Witness: I'm sorry. I don't recall that being said in the way you have just said it. There was a -- there was undoubtedly suspicion that other things than purely humanitarian aid could get on -- be put on vehicles and so forth. That was said to us on a number of occasions and not only about Ilidza." [Interpretation] Was that your comment on this video?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, or, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this page be admitted, the video and the page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like to see the question as well, so shall we admit the two pages, the previous pages of this? We don't know what this is, an answer to what question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was an answer to a question by Judge Agius. We can see the page before this, or perhaps two pages. But can we have the video admitted first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now I think it is important to get that. It's not an answer to a question by Judge Agius. Judge Agius is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. So we are going to admit two pages, and as well as the video-clip. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The video-clip will be Exhibit D1030, and the transcript, the two pages, will be Exhibit D1031.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was that what happened during your mandate, General, what we saw in the video-clip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't think it did. I just -- I don't think that video-clip was in my time. It may have been, but I'm just seeing it now. It says here, doesn't it, that this took place in 1994? In 19 -- and it goes on -- and then -- and then I acknowledge that we were being told that these things were happening when I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it an UNPROFOR convoy or a UNHCR convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a UNHCR convoy in which UNPROFOR arranged their movement and guarded them, if they needed guarding along the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you were shown another video in the Popovic et al trial. Can we see that for a second. It's a video from 1995, from the time when you were the force commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, do we need to go back to e-court? Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3228, please. The previous one was 3227. This is 1D3228.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The difficult humanitarian situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina has been used to play tricks again. "Members of the UNHCR transported ammunition for Muslim soldiers together with the food intended for the population of the Muslim enclave of Zepa. A routine control of the convoy, up-loaded at UNHCR warehouse in Pancevo, showed, at the check-point in Rogatica, that inside the flour and also in the cabs of the trucks, there was ammunition of various calibres. "Soldier of the VRS: During the control of the convoy, I think it was the fifth sack in line which I stabbed first with a knife, I saw there was something inside the flour. When I started the regular inspection, I found the ammunition. This procedure undoubtedly constitutes a most serious crime and is absolutely contrary to the mandate and nature of humanitarian missions. "Astounded or not by the ammunition found in the convoy, its leader and one of the drivers reacted like this. "Member of the convoy: Regarding the ammunition inside the trucks with flour, I don't know anything and have nothing to say. "Another member of the convoy: I don't know how ammunition found its way into the truck. I don't know what to say. I can't say anything specific. "A protest to the Office of the UNHCR in Zagreb, Belgrade and Pale was sent by the commander of the VRS, General Ratko Mladic, who asked from those responsible at these addresses to take urgent measures so that such things would not be repeated in the future. General Mladic also informed representatives of the UNHCR of the fate of the convoy that had been stopped and its personnel. The goods, says this communique by General Mladic, will be seized, and all those responsible will be subjected to appropriate legal measures. "And while we are watching the images from Rogatica that testify best about the humanitarian nature of international humanitarian organisations, what else can we say? Should we remind anyone that on the Serb side of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, they were always welcome and safe? Should we recall that the food arrives for the Muslim population with those same convoys, thanks, first and foremost, to the understanding displayed by the Serbs? Should we recall that this understanding has been betrayed for the umpteenth time? Should we ask ourselves who has the right to carry ammunition and weapons together with food? It seems we should. On whose side the truth lies, the images speak the most eloquently."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, my question is whether you agree that the side that approves convoys has the right to check the content of those convoys.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could have checked the content of those convoys, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question pertains to the side that allows the passage of convoys across its territory, the party that says that the other party can receive goods from the convoy. Can they not only check the content of the convoys, but also set the conditions as to how the aid or supplies would be sent? Wouldn't that be right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the Bosnian Serb right to do this; yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there was any question about you being able to check a convoy, but there was a question as about what was the quantities and the type of food and so forth that could be delivered. That was the business of the UNHCR and theirs to judge what was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said something similar in the Popovic et al trial. That is on page 227 of the transcript in e-court, the one that we had a few moments ago. Let me just have a look. 3204, yes, that's the document, and it's on page 17687, that is, four pages ahead. We already have the document in e-court. So you did confirm then, didn't you, that it was not necessary -- we can see the previous page as well: [In English] "... and in a particular armed conflict, when one party clears convoys through its territory so that humanitarian aid can reach the population of the other party, the authorising party is entitled to check whether or not such convoys do not carry forbidden equipment." [Interpretation] Your answer: [In English] "Yes. That's -- indeed, that was what was agreed and done."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this video?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1032, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you had meetings with us, you heard various arguments from us, so let us see, in the light of all of that, how my own statement sounds, the one that you interpreted on page 20 of your amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can those two pages of the transcript be admitted, Excellency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, you didn't ask a question about this. But you confirm what you said in Popovic et al, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add that page to the Exhibit D1031.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the amalgamated statement now, please. Just a moment, please. Let's see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The paragraph is 83.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we have it in hard copy. Please go on; the General as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you are saying, General: [In English] "With respect to the enclaves, paragraph 3 of this document reflects that Karadzic noted that he would not facilitate the movement of humanitarian aid while the Serbs were under blockade. I think this was the same argumentation used at the Jahorina meeting on March 5th -- the 5th, that as the Serbs, themselves, were, in general, under blockade, they weren't going to help anyone else. He also said he had information that the enclaves were well supplied and that the aid was being used to sustain Bosnian units. This seemed to be a general view on the part of the Serbs." [Interpretation] General, is it correct that I correctly informed you that our information was that the enclaves were well supplied and that additional supplies would only strengthen their army, and we would not allow that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that you informed me of that. I don't think I agreed at the time that they were well supplied, which is why I wanted to get the convoys in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My position is that the population was well supplied, and had there not been an armed force there, they would have been supplied, and we see that they were using this for the army. They admitted it, themselves, that it was the army that was receiving part of the aid, or, rather, they were taking part of the humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was that a question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, all right, we don't have to insist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Didn't you see, from Muslim documents, that the army took part of the humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any documents from the Bosnian side, certainly not at the time we're talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, not at the time, but we've just shown you a document of the Muslim police as to what was going on with aid in Srebrenica. But let's leave that aside and move on to page 105 -- or, rather, paragraph 105 of your statement. Paragraph 105 in e-court, or actually in the statement. Let us look at 105: [In English] "I raised the matter of the restrictions of UNPROFOR at the airport and supplies to the UN in the eastern enclaves. Karadzic confirmed that the Bosnian Serbs had to impose their own resolutions (sanctions) against the UN. Paragraph 5 of the report on the meeting notes that Karadzic said he had been convinced by the BSA that the UN had ample fuel reserves in the enclaves and that the Bosnian forces there had built up a large supply of fuel from United Nations sources. I responded that I was certain neither the Dutch nor the British contingents had supplied fuel to the defenders and that the situation was now so grave that it would soon be out of my hands." [Interpretation] And so on. Do you believe that a president should not trust his own army and his own commanders, that he should, rather, trust the other side?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly think that you should -- if you're in charge of something, you need to satisfy yourself and that you can trust what you are in command of, in charge of, and do so. And, of course, the opposing side will not give you information that you should take at face value at all. That I quite agree with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please have a look at P2245, just one paragraph. Let us see what it was that I wrote to His Excellency Mr. Akashi about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The second paragraph: "Your letter ..." [In English] "I put it to you that you --" [Interpretation] "I must say that you over-exaggerate the difficulties that exist concerning the medical supply of the eastern enclaves. According to our information, the problems are not of the magnitude that you have so freely depicted. However, where problems genuinely exist, we shall strive to eliminate them." Is it not clear, General, that I am not deceiving anyone? On the basis of information provided by our army, I assert, with a deep sense of conviction, that that was not the case and that, as a matter of fact, medicines were -- smuggling was taking place under the guise of supplying medicine. Don't you see that I'm saying this on the basis of information provided by the army?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that that is what is happening. It doesn't make it correct. The UN had people inside the enclave. And just as you trusted your sources, I would trust mine, and they were saying the opposite to you, and my people were on the inside.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This has already been admitted, anyway, so we don't have to admit it now. Can we cast a glance at P877, just one sentence. Let us see what General Mladic says on the very same topic. The 5th of March -- or, rather, the 7th of March, 1995, General Smith and General Mladic. Can we see paragraph 4. I'd like to draw your attention to that, "Humanitarian Issues - Enclaves": "Mladic asked General Smith about his impressions from his visit to Srebrenica. General Smith registered his concern over the shortages of medical supplies ..." Can we have the next page, the top of the next page. [In English] "At this stage, Mladic reported that he had cleared food and medical convoys to Srebrenica and Zepa over the last 24 hours. He then made the offer to assist with the movement of up to 450 persons from each enclave and safe passage to wherever they could be resettled by UNPROFOR ..." And so on and so on. [Interpretation] Look at paragraph 5: [In English] "Military issues and demilitarisation of the enclaves: "Mladic questioned General Simic [sic] on the military situation and the activities of B and H within the Srebrenica pocket. General Smith reported that he had not seen any weapons within the town and that he had inspected the weapon collection points."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this meeting with Mladic on the 7th of March?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you received assurances from Mladic that he had cleared the transport of medical supplies over the past 24 hours, but you did not observe any military activity in Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see what the Muslim commander says on the very same topic. 1D3136, please. 1D3136. This is an address by the commander of the Muslim army, General Delic, on the 30th of July, 1996. He is speaking about the causes of the fall in Srebrenica in July 1995. Could we please have page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The entire document is interesting, but would you please focus on this. There was this accident with the helicopter in March: "We transported the following supplies to Srebrenica, excluding Zepa, until the crash in May." And now have a look at this list of what was sent to them. Everybody can read this, so if you just scroll a bit down, you can see all the things that were sent.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These are all the things that they got, money, weapons, ammunition and so on. And look at this sentence: "Gorazde did not receive this much, and Sarajevo was defended in 1992 and 1993 with far fewer resources." So is it correct that Mladic had had correct information about military activity and the level of military supplies in Srebrenica, which is what he said to you at that meeting that you both attended?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we go back to what he said?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'm going to read out 5 from the previous document: [In English] "Mladic questioned General Smith on the military situation and the activities of B and H within the Srebrenica pocket, General Smith reported that he had not seen any weapons within the town and that he had inspected the weapon collection points." [Interpretation] Did you miss that, or did they conceal it and not even show it to you, or did you mislead Mladic on purpose?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mislead Mladic. I reported what I had seen. And the list of stuff that you've shown me of being transported, none of that would be -- would have been -- was in evidence to me when I went 'round Srebrenica on whatever the day was, 5th or 6th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But certainly you do not doubt that General Delic had provided correct information as to what he had sent to Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that's -- that what he is reporting is what he believed he had supplied to that -- those forces in Srebrenica during that year or during that time, because I think that's a list of the total supplied rather than a single supply.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1033, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now ask for P2260 for a moment. P2260. Let us look at the first page and then the second page. This is the 5th of April, 1995. Can we move on to the second page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your meeting with me; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the last sentence of the first paragraph: "On the matter of humanitarian aid, he said ..." [In English] " ... he would not facilitate the movement of humanitarian aid while the Bosnian Serbs were under blockade. He added, he had information that the enclaves were well supplied and that aid was being used to sustain the BH Army units." [Interpretation] And then, in paragraph 4. : "Karadzic clearly views the SAs, safe areas, as B and H strongholds. He made it quite clear he views the application of the safe area mandate as illegal in international law and that the SAs and EZ had been violated by the BH by their use of them for military purposes. He stated he could not accept safe areas unless it were reaffirmed that they were for the protection of civilians, that the definitions of SAs were mutually agreed and that the areas were fully demilitarised. He asked General Smith to convoy this message to the UN Secretary-General." [Interpretation] Is there anything inaccurate [Realtime transcript read in error "accurate"] in these paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 and 4, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I believe it was a correct report at the time. I continue to think it was a correct report of that conversation that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The question was: Was anything inaccurate in these paragraphs? This should be corrected on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you saying you didn't say those things?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. My question was: Was there anything incorrect in what I said here? I accept that I said this. That was my position.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with you. You can see that in the -- but that isn't the purpose of this report. The report was to report about our meeting. I am reporting to my superiors, and those who need to know, what your views were. I'm not making a judgement of them as to whether you're correct or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you confirm that this is a true record of what was said at the time of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's been admitted already. Let's see further on, 30th April, 65 ter 21110. It's, in fact, P2262.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
