utterances.text: Would you just confirm this first page? It's the minutes of the meetings in Sarajevo and in Pale on the 30th of April. Can we see page 3, please. Paragraph 12, "Other Issues": "Over dinner, Mr. Akashi, General Smith and General Janvier protested the denial of fuel convoys in the eastern enclaves. The Bosnian Serbs persisted with the line that UNPROFOR was providing supplies and fuel to the BH." [In English] "Of note, Karadzic was heard to remark, 'We regard humanitarian and UNPROFOR convoys as commercial convoys for the benefit of the Muslims. We are under double restrictions, and you can expect more restrictions.'" [Interpretation] Is this consistent with our position that UNPROFOR and civilians had enough, and shortages were occurring because the BH Army, our enemies, were being supplied from that source, and they shouldn't have been there in the first place?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was consistent with your sanctioning of the UN and UNPROFOR for those reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, General, that the commander, I believe, of the British battalion from Gorazde wrote to his superior command that Muslims in Gorazde were demanding that he treat them like Oric was treated, that they receive 50 per cent of UN fuel? I can find that letter, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if the -- if you can. I'd like to know its date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's spring 1995. Now, I don't have time. But the point is: The Muslims in Gorazde were pressuring him to do the same thing that was being done in Srebrenica, saying that Oric, in Srebrenica, was receiving 50 per cent of the UN fuel ration?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may have been the case. I don't recall the letter, but I can -- I can imagine such an approach being made to that commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see P2266. Yes. This is a meeting of 21st May, 1995, just before the bombing. Point 2: "The atmosphere was open and productive. Karadzic left immediately after the meeting for the forthcoming Bosnian Serb Assembly in Banja Luka." And so on. And now: "It appears that isolation continues to have an effect on him and he shows an increasing conviction in his own arguments." Let's now look at page 2. [In English] "He maintained the Bosnian Serbs wished a negotiated settlement as opposed to one achieved by military means. It is his belief that the United Nations --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, where are we?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Top of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I see, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "... the UN should remain in Bosnia to implement a future political settlement. He also asserted that any change in the UN mandate must be done in consultation with both parties." [Interpretation] In the middle of this para 4: [In English] "Again he asserted he could not respect the safe area mandates, as the enclaves were effectively safe havens for the Army of BH. He said he expected the BH to attempt to break out of one of the enclaves, and he expected UNPROFOR to be caught in the cross-fire. The enclaves, he said, are 'a time bomb about to explode.' He maintained the UN should get out, but also that UNHCR should be safe to remain. UNPROFOR presence, he stated, was welcome 'only if the enclaves are demilitarised and become safe areas for the civilian population.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, my question is: Was that the first time you heard that from me or was that our constant demand, that safe areas are intended for civilians, they should be only for civilians, and, as such, they would be protected? Didn't we constantly warn the United Nations about what was going on?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You -- this is not the first time the sentiments in that paragraph were expressed by you and General Mladic. I think it's the first time, hence it being in inverted commas, something like "a time bomb about to explode," was said, but the sentiment you had certainly expressed before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see 1D652. 65 ter 10652. We'll see it in a moment. It's about a meeting between representatives of the Secretary-General in Split on 9 June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember attending that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see page 5. The entire document is very interesting, it should be interesting to everyone, but now we don't have time to go through it all. Paragraph 24, the last sentence: "If we are not prepared to fight, we will always be stared down by the BSA." [In English] "We are already over the Mogadishu line; the Serbs do not view us as peacekeepers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you remind us, what is the Mogadishu line?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mogadishu is a town -- city in Somalia in which there had been a well-publicised event involving the United States armed forces, who were acting alongside, but not part of, the United Nations. The -- my predecessor, General Rose, had used the phrase to try and describe the -- at least this is my understanding of what he was trying -- what he -- why he used the phrase, to try and describe the point at which you move from a pure peacekeeping situation, where you are standing between the warring factions, and the warring factions have agreed to your presence and have agreed to stop fighting. And he was very concerned that -- in his time that the situation around him and the instructions he was receiving was such that he would find himself going over this line. And I am using his terminology in this remark.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, the representatives of the Secretary-General says: "Can we return (back over the line)?" And you say: "Only by either doing nothing, or by showing an absolute readiness to fight, including going over the top. That is possible because the BSA has its hands full with the BH." And then General Janvier says -- which of these two options, doing nothing or an absolute readiness to fight, was supported by you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was offering the alternatives at that point in this debate, as I recall it. My point is that we have a job to do, to deliver the aid and oversee the safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And General Janvier says: "I insist we will never have the possibility of combat ..." [In English] "... of imposing our will on the Serbs. The only possible way is to go through political negotiations - that is the only way we can fulfill our mandate." [Interpretation] The last sentence of 28: "If heavy weapons leave the zone, problems will be created for the Serbs because of the BH infantry." Isn't it clear that General Janvier understands that there's much more infantry on the Bosnian side than the Serb side and that heavy weapons are the only element of strategic balance?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we both understood that. And I think I explained it earlier this week in describing my thesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at para 30: [In English] "It is just for this that we must establish contact with the Serbs, to show -- explain to them that there are just some things that they cannot do." [Interpretation] And you say: "My judgement is that they will not listen." Janvier says: "I have a different approach. Once again, the Serbs are in a very favourable political position, and that is something they will not want to compromise." [In English] "The external political situation is such that the Serbs will come to understand the benefits of co-operation. Unless there is a major provocation by the BH, the Serbs will not act." [Interpretation] Do you see -- do you agree that General Janvier believed the same thing that we were saying; if we are not provoked, if we are not attacked, we will not attack?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see what is written there. I can't answer for General Janvier any further than that. But he is clearly of a different view to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But he was one of your commanding officers?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this meeting is taking place on the 9th of June, and on the 15th of June the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina started a major offensive in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, please. General Smith: "It's the interplay between the Serbs and the BH that might produce something." [In English] "The Serbs' enemy is the BH, and they want us neutralised, not as an enemy."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the time, it was your understanding and your position, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The point I'm making to my commander and the SRSG is that we have these two objectives; one, to deliver the aid, and the other, to oversee the safe areas and the exclusion zones. And this leads us into what I'm referring to there as enforcement obligations. And this situation is essentially contradictory, and I wanted my commanders to understand that I thought we would be forced into a decision if we didn't start to organise our thinking and get our intentions clear, we would be forced into a decision within a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that you will then engage in a hostility with the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The potential was there, and it was that that I was warning him of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's see what General Janvier says at 36: [In English] "With the reaction force, we would be able to impose tactical superiority in Sarajevo; if he had a conflict, Mladic's tanks would have a problem. But that is not their task. As long as the enclaves continue to exist, we will be neutralised to an extent. In New York, I said that the BH Army should defend the safe areas, they are strong enough to do it. That was not well received at all. "There followed a brief discussion of the BSA detainees, during which it was agreed that they would not be released until the UN hostages are released ..." [Interpretation] So Janvier believed that there was absolutely no need for you to defend the enclaves because the enclaves were so well armed and capable of defending themselves; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He appears to be saying that in -- in that paragraph, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he goes on to say: "There was also a discussion of UNPROFOR resupply convoys to the eastern enclaves; the FC said Mladic had assured him they could take place, but through the FRY," the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, "because there would be resistance if the convoys passed through Pale." Would you explain this? Do you agree that Mladic can already foresee that people being enraged, as they are, there would be problems?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that. I see that Mladic agreed or assured him that they would take place, and through the -- through Yugoslavia rather than through BSA territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: General, could I interpose. One interpretation of this document seems to be that you were taking a rather longer view than that which General Janvier was expressing, in terms of considering the eventual consequences of policy, to put it neutrally. Is that a fair interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I was. My memory of this is -- is that the -- we had this disagreement that was settled here with me being given the instruction that after this, the force protection was the primary consideration, rather than doing what we'd been told to do in our orders, mandate, whatever you call it. And my arguments were rather more in the longer term, yes, than the absolutely short term, but it would require fairly short-term, you know, actions to start to be taken in the near future if we were to be ready for that long-term eventuality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: If I remember rightly, that's a rather Wellingtonian [Realtime transcript read in error "Orwellian"] view.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's very flattering. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To us, then, isn't that right, General, it wasn't easy to be in our shoes; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was having quite enough trouble in my own shoes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I think I just need to correct the transcript. I see that my reference to Lord Wellington has come out as a reference to George Orwell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could have been Orwellian as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That might have been the case but it certainly wouldn't be my suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then I also withdraw my remarks that I meant George Orwell too. Can we now see D136, just one sentence. Can the previous document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1034, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D136. It's already an exhibit of the Defence. The English version will suffice on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report from the 2nd Corps of the BH Army in Tuzla for the 27th of June, 1995. Information obtained by radio-reconnaissance, addressed to the 28th Division Command, the Intelligence Section: "In the morning hours of 26 June 1995, our forces attacked from the Srebrenica area and set fire to the village of Visnjica. According to as yet undetermined -- unverified information, the Chetniks had casualties among the civilian population." Did you have any information about civilian losses in the village of Visnjica?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this stage, I doubt, but this was reported to us, I think, by the Bosnian Serb Army at a later date. I certainly knew about it when we are discussing Srebrenica in Geneva in the early part of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to draw your attention to paragraph 150 of your statement, page 37. Do you agree that the second half of June was marked by an offensive of the Muslim forces in Sarajevo that lasted until early July?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What bit of my statement are you referring me to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to establish a chronological connection. The first half of June was the crisis involving the taking of prisoners among your men. The second half of June passed, and it was marked by an offensive of the Muslim forces in Sarajevo; is that correct? It's not in your statement, but --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes, there was an attack out of Sarajevo by the Bosnian forces around about the middle of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the 28th Division carried out simultaneous attacks, with the objective of spreading the Serbian forces thin and making things easier for the 1st Corps of the Muslim army in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember knowing it, but I dare say we -- our reporting would have picked up the increase in attacks elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope that after the break, we'll be able to show that Muslim document. However, this is 150 of your statement: [In English] "July was dominated by the fall of the enclaves. The attack on Srebrenica started on the 6th of July and was seen at the time as a local affair and as a punishment for attacks by the Bosnians from inside the enclaves. The attack intensified during 8, 9, 10th July." [Interpretation] Is that correct? You saw that as a local affair and as a punishment for attacks by Bosnians from the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our interpretation at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have a look at your statement from 1996, 1D3147. 1D3147, page 9. While this is being found, 1D3195, could we have that, please, your interview with the Dutch Institute. 1D3195. We've already had that. I think it's been admitted in its entirety, all 16 pages. Page 6, please, paragraph 18. Paragraph 18 in this document. Could you go back now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You've got the Dutch copy up, and I can't do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sladojevic speaks Dutch, and that's why it's that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's change into English. This is a Dutch version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just see the previous page so that we see where paragraph 18 begins: [In English] "The first meeting with Mladic after the fall of Srebrenica, on Sunday (16 July) was also attended by Milosevic, Bildt, Akashi and Janvier (although --" [Interpretation] Next page, please. Everybody can read that, so let's look at this part: "According to Mladic ..." [In English] "... the BSA attacked Srebrenica because of constant 'hit and run' operations from within the enclave. The BiH Army fled, and suddenly Mladic and his troops were in the centre of Srebrenica. According to Mladic, all this happened totally unexpectedly. He was sorry that a Dutch soldier had been killed. He was furious about the aeroplane bomb that nearly hit him. Smith then said, 'It's a pity I missed you.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't actually think I said that, but I may have. Who -- is this a summary of later reports or the report of somebody who was there at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we see the first page? It seems to be your statement given to NIOD, the Dutch Institute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So this is -- this is what I said to them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let us see the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 12th of January, 2000; right? Do you recognise the first page?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is their report of this interview?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Then that's what I said to them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see how you describe it in your book. Can we have 1D3196, and then page 12 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for your information, Mr. Karadzic, this interview hasn't been admitted into evidence. What we admitted is his interview or his words at the Dutch Parliament.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, let it be. However, this is part of the transcript, so we can use the transcript. 1D -- oh, yes, right. It is page 351 in the book, page 12 in e-court. I think that should be it: [In English] "So Mladic, rather than Karadzic ..." [No interpretation]: [In English] "I also gained the impression that the Bosnian Serbs then saw Mladic, rather than Karadzic, as a personification of their struggle. Towards me and the UN, he appeared a confident, arrogant bully who rated UNPROFOR as a hindrance rather than a threat. One of these meetings took place in Vlasenica on the 7th of March, when I was on the way back from Srebrenica. The content of the meeting was well reflected in a subsequent report." [No interpretation]: [In English] "At a meeting, General Mladic indicated that he was dissatisfied with the safe area regime, and that he might take military action against the eastern enclaves. He also said that, should such attacks take place, he would nevertheless guarantee the safety of the Bosniak population of those areas. The UNPROFOR commander warned him not to attack the enclaves, stating that such action would almost certainly lead to international military intervention against the Serbs. General Mladic was dismissive."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, either on the basis of this or on the basis of something else, you saw Mladic, first and foremost, as an arrogant bully; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I read something out to you, how you viewed that meeting? P877. We've already had that on our screens in e-court: [In English] "General Smith replied that although he understood the military reasons for such an action, he warned Mladic that such an action would be interpreted as an attack on the UN safe areas and condemned by the international community, and, furthermore, that such an action could not be in the best interests of the Bosnian Serbs." [Interpretation] It's around the middle. You can see it, "General Smith," et cetera. Here it is. It's the lower part of this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, this is the -- Baxter's report of the meeting between Mladic and I in Vlasenica, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And in your book, you said something similar; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to -- now, what are you referring me to? I'm looking at paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. [In English] "General Smith replied that although he understood ..." [Interpretation] Do you see that part where the cursor is now?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the entire page, please. Could you zoom out a bit so that we see the top of the page as well. Just a moment, please: [In English] "At this stage, Mladic reported that he had cleared food and medicine convoys to Srebrenica and Zepa over the last 24 hours. He then made the offer to assist with the movement of up to 450 persons from each enclave and their safe passage ...," and so on. [Interpretation] Further on, the position is everything is fine if there are no attacks. However, if attacks take place, he has to prevent them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this look like an arrogant bully, the way you had seen him?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the -- how one affects the other. And this -- I report my impression of him as a person, and here's that person saying what he's going to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, General, on the basis of your experience, can a mad person be held criminally liable?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You don't have to answer the question, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then let us look at page 12 of your book -- or, rather, 350 in the book, itself, but it's page 12. Page 12 of the book. 1D3196. It is P already or -- no. It's 350 in the book, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Take a look at this. You are describing who was there on your side, and then you say: "Opposite us ..." [In English] "... were the three Ks, Karadzic, Krajisnik and Koljevic (classified in my head as the mad, the bad, and the loony)." [Interpretation] What do you say to that, General, your view of us?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I thought. I decided that -- my definitions were based largely on the film of "The Good, The Bad And The Ugly." And the "mad" is I thought that you, as I've said, and we've seen other bits of evidence, might appear completely rational, but you were basing it on a world that wasn't shared by anybody else. And perhaps we should leave the characterisation of the other two, particularly of the unfortunate Professor Koljevic, to another place and time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, General, you have an advantage because I cannot make jokes like this, because it would be a diagnosis, since I'm a psychiatrist. Any joke of mine on that account would be a diagnosis. Well, let us leave that aside. How did you view the Muslim leadership, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to just -- can I just correct the account of my answer? I said that while you appeared completely rational, it was based -- so it was based on a world that nobody else was sharing, or it wasn't shared by anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As you're not a psychiatrist, I forgive you. But could you tell us how you viewed the Muslim leadership?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall having the same classifications, but I didn't think they were being completely worldly, either, on occasions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I see the time. Thank you. Excellency, is it the right time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long do you expect, at this stage, your cross-examination to last?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As long as possible. I asked for 40 hours, and I got 30 per cent of that. So this is, indeed, a very important witness and participant, so please give me as much time as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll see. Half an hour. We'll resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Karadzic, Judge Baird has a question for General Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: General, as I studied your evidence last night, I realised that there are two small areas for which I would like clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, time is of the essence, so I shall endeavour to paraphrase as much as possible. All right? Now, as respects the no-fly zone infringements, you stated that -- in answer to Dr. Karadzic, that on occasions, aircraft had landed at one of the alternative airstrips in the vicinity of Tuzla. You said: "We, in UNPROFOR, never got to the bottom of it, and to who was responsible, and how they avoided the NATO no-fly zone." Now, when you said, General, that you never got to the bottom of it, and who was responsible, and how they avoided the no-fly zone, can you tell us what you did in an endeavour to get to the bottom of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The -- stop me, please, if I'm telling you something you know already, but the -- NATO ran the no-fly zone, which was the very first involvement of NATO in this region -- in these operations. They flew an aeroplane called an AWACS and that monitored all flights over the no-fly zone over Bosnia-Herzegovina and could then vector a combat air patrol to shoot down an aeroplane that they -- wasn't cleared and they could recognise as being transgressing the zone. The -- they had great difficulty in picking up the flights of helicopters, and we, the UN, had helicopters as well, and so there were plenty of evidence that helicopters were avoiding the no-fly zone because of their potential confusion with a UN aircraft that hadn't been recognised or authorised, and the potential of shooting down a UN aeroplane was high, and, secondly, because of the difficulties of the radars in picking up those targets when they were flown very low to the ground. When -- at about the same time Mladic is complaining to me that these flights are taking place, we have the incidents of the UN forces in the Tuzla area reporting similar events. You could -- they weren't precisely the same reports, but they were sufficiently close to see that these were, if not one-and-the-same incidents, similar incidents. Tuzla was a -- Tuzla Air Base was a former Yugoslavian Air Force base and consisted of a substantial surfaced runway, with the normal facilities of military huts and so forth around it, and then at least two other alternative strips that were off to -- some distance away. The UN force was around the and based on the substantial concreted airstrip, and what was happening, and being reported by Mladic to me, was that one or other of these alternative strips was being used to land aeroplanes on. And we had a number of reports from our own people of aeroplanes being seen if not landing, looking as though they're about to land or just having taken off. At no stage did we get an identification of the aeroplane or with any confidence of its size or load. All of these reports were put back to NATO, who said they didn't know -- they weren't picking any of these things up and they hadn't spotted them to stop them. And there was then a joint -- a party of NATO people came out with the UN, my people. This is sometime in February, I think. And a thoroughly inconclusive investigation was carried out, during which the NATO people were saying things like, You're not -- you're mis-identifying something, and we're saying, We know an aircraft when we see one, and something is happening here. And, what's more, the Serbs are telling us something's happening here, and we're not the only observers of this. And that's where it rested. The incidents dropped away, if I recall, once we started to complain, and I don't recall them occurring again thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed, for that answer, General. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask, Your Excellency, that these pages of the book, 350 and 351, be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now call 1D3139 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I'm afraid that you were not always so well informed about all the goings on. We'll now take a look to see what kind of co-operation the 28th Division had with your units behind your back, while Pale was being bombed. Look at what this Muslim officer, Esad Hadzic, is writing. It's strictly confidential, addressed to the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Look at the beginning, for instance. 30th May, Pale is being bombed: "A meeting was held with the representatives of the Dutch battalions in Srebrenica. "It was announced that all the important issues of the enclave and UNPROFOR's mandate would be discussed at this meeting. "The meeting commenced as scheduled and was attended by Major Franken, battalion deputy commander, and Warrant Officer Rave on behalf of the UNPROFOR Command. At the beginning of the meeting, they told us they would be frank, to the point, that they wanted the meeting to be at the highest level of confidentiality, they did not want any military observers to be present at the meeting ...," et cetera. Was this secret meeting from you, too?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember an account of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see the next page. We'll tender this so everyone can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now it says: "Our proposal was to be somewhere close." That's what Franken said: [In English] "It is our opinion that --" [Interpretation] No, that's the conclusion. No, before this: [In English] "However, our aim is to defend ourselves --" [Interpretation] The sentence begins with different words in English: [In English] "They suggested -- they suggested --" [Interpretation] See it in the middle of the page?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then goes on "we," "be somewhere." Is that the next -- have I got the right place suggested? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Precisely: "They suggested that we, UNPROFOR, be somewhere near them to help, and we agreed to it in case of extreme need, but in camouflage, both vis-a-vis them and the Chetniks. They proposed, and we agreed that the division command representative," that means the 28th Division Command representative, "visit the critical posts with their representative and that they agree on the eventual positions of our forces in case of need, so that they could successfully guide the air force for close support against Serbian targets and so that our men would not find themselves in the operations zone of their anti-infantry and anti-armoured artillery weapons against the Chetniks. When we asked about the fate of the weapons surrendered to UNPROFOR, the major replied resolutely that the moment the Chetniks start their land attack on the enclave, the ammunition depot with the stored weapons is open to you and you can take it for your use. "It is our opinion that the meeting was frank, well intentioned, and that we received useful information." Did they hold this back from you, and did they have good reasons to hold it back from you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall any such meeting being reported to me, and I don't know their reasoning. I can't speak for their reasons to hide it from me, if they thought I -- they were doing that on purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here that Franken asked the meeting to be very confidential. Does this indicate a profound war alliance against the Serbs? While you protest against us, that we did not return our weapons, you're offering them to take their weapons and to act jointly with them on the front-line?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is -- it's dependent, I think, you'll find, on the eventuality of you attacking. But, yes, he's saying that he -- he's reported as saying that when it -- when the attack starts -- when your attack starts on the enclave, then the depot with the stored weapons is open.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it also says that they will be together in position so that they, Dutch soldiers, could guide air-strikes to Serb targets: [In English] "... could successfully guide the air force for close air support against Serbian targets --"

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What they're saying is they don't want the Bosnians in the way, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to read the whole document, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to read the first page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question would be whether this kind of meeting was unusual.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can -- my first question is -- that they didn't want any military observers, and I'm wondering, since there are -- now I've gone and touched the screen. It's gone away. They've -- whether that refers to UNMOs, because otherwise there's military presence. Thank you. Yes. I would -- I would think it unusual, but the probability of such circumstance -- you know, the circumstances immediately after that, the events of the hostage-taking and the bombing, would make it more probable. I can recognise the circumstances. I'd also -- there's no reason, particularly, why it should have been reported to me, because the level to which that Srebrenica reported was to the Sector North-East commander in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1035, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, could we now take up the nature of the Serb occupation of Srebrenica? You agree with the fact that the attack on Srebrenica was a reaction to attacks from the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the immediate cause, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see 1D3196, page 16. Page 359: [In English] "I agreed ..." [Interpretation] I'll find the passage now. The seventh line from the top: [In English] "I agreed with the assessment that this attack was in reaction to those 'provocations' and might amount to further ..." And so on and so on. [Interpretation] Tell us, you were not the only one who were of this opinion, and there were other people who thought so, and you only agreed with them; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- I'm either in Geneva or on leave, and that's what we were -- that's what I think -- my memory is that that's what we were being told, and what I was hearing was what I was agreeing with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now see 1D3190.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, would you tell us: Who was General Nicolai?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Nicolai was the -- my Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at the letter sent by General Nicolai to the Muslim army commander Rasim Delic on the 9th of July, 1995. That's right in the middle of the crisis in Srebrenica. General Nicolai writes to Delic: "You will also receive a letter from the acting commander, General Gobillard, protesting against the operations undertaken yesterday in the area of Srebrenica by your forces, who shot and killed a Dutch member of the peacekeeping forces." Did you know about this protest?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that it was taking place, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Third paragraph, second sentence, says: "The attempts of your forces to keep the observation posts in their place and attack the members of the withdrawing peacekeeping forces have only rendered the already dangerous and unstable situation even more complicated." Does this indicate that the observers wanted to withdraw, and the Muslim army tried to prevent them?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it appears to say in there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So that agreement from the 30th of May no longer applied. Now, look at the rest of the text: "In response to your other two requests ..." That's the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can we go back a moment? I don't recall an agreement of the 30th of May. I don't know that they agreed to anything. At the end of -- at the end of that document, I think the commander is saying that he will -- has learned a great deal and is -- will deploy his forces according to their interests on the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I'm referring to the previous document, where the local forces agreed with the political and military leadership of Srebrenica. It's the document that we looked at a moment ago, that secret meeting that they kept secret from you too. So, on the 30th of May, they agreed on joint action, and already on the 9th of July, your observers wanted to withdraw from their observation posts, and the Muslim army is trying to stop them?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am objecting at the moment, at least, to your interpretation of what was said by the Bosnian reporting on that meeting of the 30th of May. I don't think there was an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that Muslim officer says that there was an agreement, but let's go back to this letter: "In response to your other two requests, I can inform you that NATO air support was provided during combat, but that due to the technical difficulties which prevented target identification, criteria for using close air support ...," et cetera. What requests were made by General Delic to General Nicolai? One request was for NATO air-strikes. What was the other request?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We strongly objected to the attitude and treatment UNPROFOR gave to the Muslim army by receiving orders from them and their wish lists. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was that your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question is: Was it appropriate for UNPROFOR to receive orders, wish lists, from a Muslim general?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the -- without understanding the letter that's being responded to, I can't -- I don't know what he's answering, what these requests are. So -- and I can only work off the document, since I was still on leave at that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1036, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And do you like to add page 359 of the book?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not necessarily. It's only about one sentence. Now let's see 1D3183. 1D3183. We have a translation. I'll use the Serbian hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an intercept of a conversation between General Gvero and General Nicolai. This was recorded at 1610 hours, when this UNPROFOR soldier was killed by the Muslims. Let's look at this: "'The Muslims killed a UN soldier,' says Gvero, 'and we provided protection for your soldiers who were in danger and who were our guests.'" Do you know that we gave hospitality to your soldiers whom the Muslims tried to force to remain in their positions?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the details of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A bit further below, General Gvero says: "Tell General Nicolai that we have nothing to halt, such as shelling UN positions, because we've never done that at all. Secondly, we are not targeting the civilian population ...," et cetera. And then further below, it says: "It's not true that we're opening fire against UN positions anywhere. General Nicolai should remember that the same claim was made regarding Gorazde, and it was later proven wrong. He should remember how the Muslims complained in Gorazde and some other places, like Bihac, for example, and it later turned out that all that was incorrect. The same Muslim propaganda is under way again. Don't let the UN buy their lies again, don't let that happen, because time will show what is true and what isn't." Do you know that we steadfastly repeated that Muslim propaganda and falsehoods are being readily bought by the whole international community and were being turned against us?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I put that as a question, but let me rephrase it. Did you know, for example, that in Gorazde, there was this war trick played by the Muslim side; something was ascribed to the Serbs that was not actually done by them?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That didn't only happen in Gorazde, or it certainly happened the other way 'round too. I don't understand. Did Gvero initiate this call, and at what -- at what point in this -- is this taking place? Is this when he's saying in the previous letter -- Nicolai is saying in the previous -- the letter you showed me previously that the -- they tried to fly close air support? Is that what this is referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was his letter to General Delic, and here he is discussing the same matter with General Gvero. And Gvero is telling him that their soldiers were killed by Muslims -- by the Muslims, and General Nicolai confirms that in a letter. Now, General Gvero is saying throughout, We are not doing what we are being blamed for, those are tricks, ruses. And in the last paragraph, he says --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you were attacking. You told me you were attacking at that time. I am really confused about what it is you're trying to ask me a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the way it is: General Gvero is claiming that we are not attacking your people or civilians, although that is what the reports say. And in the last paragraph, he says that if General Nicolai's soldiers are under threat, let them cross over to the Serb side and they are going to be safe there. The point is that the Muslims had killed the soldier and that our soldiers are offering protection to your soldiers. Also, we are not shelling UN positions, or civilians, the civilian population. That is the usual propaganda of the Muslim army, as was the case with Gorazde and so on and so forth. And in the last paragraph, he says to General Nicolai that if his people are under threat, they can cross over to the Serb side. That is the core of the matter.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And if -- I have every reason to suppose that that intercept is a correct record of this conversation. And the other document says that the close air support mission had been called and it had not been able to find the target, and so the aeroplanes flew away, which appears to be, if these two things are -- reports are that closely related, it appears to be what he then says at the end, the aeroplanes are departing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree, then, that the assessment of your command was similar to General Gvero's as presented during this conversation?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I have no evidence, from what you've shown me, to suppose that it's the same.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We'll go back to that. Let us please have a look at the end of this document. It's probably on the next page. Just scroll down a bit, and then you can see "Gvero," "Karadzic." They claim here that Gvero and Karadzic talked and that Gvero was informing Karadzic about this conversation with Nicolai.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, General, that at the time I had very poor relations with some of my officers, and they were the worst with Gvero? We did not communicate at all, and I reprimanded him in public, including at sessions of Parliament. Do you know that it was a very poor relationship, no contacts whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of the extent of this relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there any confirmation here that this is a conversation with Karadzic? Please look at this document, where he says: "I told him, Mr. President." Do you know how many presidents there are in our part of the world; president of Parliament, president of the Municipality, president of the Hunting Society, and so on and so forth. Is there any proof of this being a conversation with President Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the document, other than it says "Mr. President," and it's the sort of subject I would expect you -- of being a conversation that might easily take place between you and a general. But without knowing more about the intercept and what the telephone numbers or their frequencies were, or whatever, I'd be pressed to tell you more than that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll put it being marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1037, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have D137, quite simply to see what the assessment of the UN was in relation to what was going on; what was going on in the enclaves, that is, in relation to what Gvero's assessment was, although I so often disagreed with him. 1D3 -- actually, just D, D137. Yes, that's it, that's the document. Can we now please have page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: UNPROFOR Headquarters Zagreb; right? Please look at this paragraph that says: "Similar ...," et cetera: [In English] "Similar to what happened in Gorazde, spring 1994, the BH can attempt to draw UNPROFOR, including the Rapid Reaction Forces or NATO into the conflict on the BH side. "Sudden abandoning of positions along the confrontation line, the simulation of a collapse of the enclave or alarming reports from Bosnian side on the situation in the enclave will be indicators for this. A stronger involvement of the international community could be interpreted by the Bosnian Serb Army as an incentive to step up operations and try to eliminate the enclave, as well as retaliate against UN forces." [Interpretation] So there's no doubt that this is from the Zagreb headquarters, it's a telegram from there; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's their daily situation report. But I didn't get the date. What day was this on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 10th, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This has already been admitted. No need to have it admitted now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Also, it seems that your higher command has assessments that are similar to those of General Gvero; that is to say, ruses of war, tricks intended at drawing the UN into a war against the Serbs. Right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They seem that the -- to arrive at a similar result, but Gvero isn't suggesting any of those things there except that the Bosnians are blaming the Bosnian Serbs for what is happening, and Gvero is saying, You're not doing these things.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D3168, please. It's a letter sent by General Mladic to General Smith, 1D3168.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So that's the letter dated the 10th of July: "General, sir, I have received your letter from the 9th of July, 1995. The Srebrenica enclave has not been demilitarised according to the agreements of the 19th of April and the 8th of May, 1993. The Muslims have not handed over the weapons, mine/explosive and combative means to UNPROFOR. The Muslim forces have abused the special status of Zepa in the presence of your forces for preparing and performing terrorist and other combat activities against the Serb population and the territory of the Republika Srpska. "I remind you that up to now, the Muslim forces have killed a hundred and wounded over 200 Serb civilians by attacking them and through infiltrated sabotage-terrorist groups." And so on and so forth: "Even UNPROFOR members were not spared of their ill intentions. Although they protected them, your forces became their victims too." Do you remember receiving this letter from General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it there when I got back. I don't remember -- sorry. I imagine that the -- he's responding to a letter from my deputy or my Chief of Staff that he's referring to on the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1038, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A few moments ago, we saw that assessment of your forces about the collapse of the defence, about creating conditions for bringing the international community into the war. Do you agree that Srebrenica was abandoned and that Mladic all of a sudden found himself in Srebrenica, where there was no one?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with that. There were lots of people there and DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, General, let's see what Carl Bildt says, Ambassador Bildt. 1D301 -- 3201. And we'll go back to this document. Actually, can we have this letter admitted? 1D3201, can we see that now. The letter has already been admitted, and that confused me a bit. 1D3201. This is from Carl Bildt's book, page 57. It's page 17 in e-court, and in the book, itself, it is page 57: [In English] "The defending forces of Bosnian Muslim ABiH - the so-called 28th --" [Interpretation] Over here, it says "82nd," but it should be the 28th: [In English] "... was not putting up any resistance. Later, it was revealed that they had been ordered by the Sarajevo commanders not to defend Srebrenica, but to try to go -- to break through in the direction of the Tuzla area with their soldiers, their men, and their political and military leadership. And this they were now busy preparing for. The women and children were to be left to the protection of and evacuation by the UN." [Interpretation] Further on, it says: [In English] "Within an hour of the return of F-16s to their base in Italy, Mladic's soldiers entered the town of Srebrenica itself. It was empty. The women and children had been told to go to the Dutch UN base at Potocari a few kilometres down the valley, and most of the men had by then already started their operation to break out, leave the enclave and head west."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, do you recall that all of Srebrenica had been emptied? The army left in order to break through, and the population was told to go to Potocari so that they would be protected and evacuated by the UN?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you -- narrowly defined, I was answering your question about it wasn't empty because I was referring to Srebrenica, the whole enclave, not the town. Yes, I believe it was empty by the time the Bosnian Serb Army entered the built-up area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us just have a look at this further on: [In English] "Only minutes after the news broke, I was meeting Foreign Minister Sacirbey in one of those charmless, half-furnished rooms given to the members of the European Parliament at the Palais de l'Europe in Strasbourg. Surprisingly, I was more upset by what had happened then. He seemed to be -- his calm reactions and his controlled arguments still seem to me to be a mysterious piece of the Srebrenica puzzle. "Srebrenica, he said, had always been a problem for his government. They knew that a peace settlement would mean the loss of the enclaves. So from this point of view, what had happened made things easier." [Interpretation] Did you know that Srebrenica was a burden for the Bosnian Government and that they thought that the enclaves could not go on if there were to be a peace agreement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this page be admitted? The first part has been confirmed, and it is in accordance with what General Smith knows, himself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That the built-up area of Srebrenica was emptied -- empty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was in the transcript. Why do we need to admit a third person's book? I think that's sufficient. You read out the passage, and the general agreed to the extent he could, and that's sufficient. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can we now have 65 ter 19719. 19719, 19719.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, now we're supposed to deal with the fate of the civilian population in Srebrenica. Let us see whether they were ethnically cleansed, as the indictment says, or was it something else that had happened, as suggested by Bildt and as shown by UN documents. Do you agree that this is a telegram to Annan from Ambassador Akashi on the 19th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I made a mistake. It was a slip of the tongue. Can we have the next page, please. The next page, B, Ambassador Akashi says: "The UNHCR ..." [In English] " ... reports that 80 to 90 per cent of the population of Srebrenica (total pop is 40.000) are displaced persons who fled fighting earlier in the war, thus they do not have longstanding ties to homes and property in the enclave, and will probably be interested in leaving for Tuzla. An UNHCR local staff member in Srebrenica reported today that virtually everyone in the enclave wished to leave." [Interpretation] Can we see this other sentence: [In English] "Following consultations with the Bosnian Government and in order to avoid a continuing humanitarian catastrophe, agreement will be solicited from the Bosnian Serbs to allow all residents of Srebrenica, including all men, to leave for Tuzla if they so wish." [Interpretation] A bit further down: [In English] "UNPROFOR, with the support of UNHCR, will also endeavour to reach agreement with the Bosnian Serbs to escort any convoy or refugees from Srebrenica to Tuzla. It is likely that the BSA will resist this." [Interpretation] Were you aware of this report of Ambassador Akashi's, sent to Annan?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure I saw a copy of this on my return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, General, that we were surprised when none of the residents were there? When the army withdrew, we didn't find anyone in Srebrenica, and we were opposed to that, having the entire population leave.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page, please. [In English] "UNHCR will immediately begin negotiations with the Bosnian Serbs for: "1. The provision of emergency food and medical supplies for the people of Srebrenica, particularly the wounded and the approximately 25.000 displaced by the fighting; "2. The safe, rapid and orderly departure from Srebrenica of all those people, including men of military age, for Tuzla, beginning with the evacuation of the wounded on an emergency basis. This will be a massive logistics operation, beginning potentially as early as 13th of July. Although modalities for determining the free will of the people for the departure are yet to be decided, they will in any case be rough and approximate, perhaps as simple as anyone coming to a bus and stating they want to leave." [Interpretation] A bit further down: [In English] "We can, however, expect resistance from the BSA to a rapid and safe departure of all those wishing to leave." [Interpretation] A bit further down: [In English] "The fact that the BSA will have practical difficulties controlling 40.000 people may mitigate against its desire to prolong or exacerbate the plight of the Srebrenica population." [Interpretation] The last page now, just one sentence, please: [In English] "All those wishing to leave Srebrenica for Tuzla must be allowed to do so under UNHCR care."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this is on the 11th, the exact date when the Serb side entered Srebrenica. Do you agree that the initiative for the evacuation of civilians was launched with the UN by the Muslim side and that Ambassador Akashi's estimate is that that request should be met and the Serbs should be asked to agree to that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You -- I don't recall you reading out and I haven't noticed what you've just asked me to agree to in those terms. What I heard and -- think I've heard and read is the UN preparing to carry out an evacuation of a very large number of people that are clustering around the Dutch in Potocari. I didn't see that the -- there'd been yet a direct request for their evacuation by the Bosnian Government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at the second page of this document. Let me remind you: [In English] "Following consultations with the Bosnian Government, and in order to avoid a continuing humanitarian catastrophe, agreement will be solicited from the Bosnian Serbs to allow all residents of Srebrenica, including all men, to leave for Tuzla if they so wish." [Interpretation] So when consulting the Bosnian Government what should be done, they came to the conclusion that the Serbs should be asked to enable the evacuation of civilians, all the civilians who want to go to Tuzla. Is it clear now?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's clear they had consultations. The reason that I'm -- wanted to go back and see what had been said is because when I get to -- into Sarajevo on the -- I think it's the 13th, I am having great difficulty in getting anyone in the Bosnian Government to have any sense of responsibility for these people at all, and it doesn't chime very comfortably with what you're saying was being discussed between Zagreb and this government on the 11th. The document in which I'm having difficulty was presented earlier in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude from this text clearly that we -- it is expected that we would resist such evacuation? These are talks between Ambassador Akashi with the Muslims, on the one hand, and his report to Annan as to what he was about to do and what his proposal was, and did he actually expect that the Serb side would resist this?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see anything or you didn't read me anything to say that we -- that Zagreb headquarters was anticipating that you would resist the evacuation of refugees. There is reference to -- that you would resist the movements of people in certain directions. I'm trying to find the bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "It is likely -- "

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: "... to escort any refugees from Srebrenica to --" It will be the escorting of the convoys that you would resist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, General, that the Serb side -- the Serb Army did not have any vehicles at its disposal and that it had actually to try and obtain them haphazardly only as late as the 12th and the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I remember a large number of buses were produced. How they were produced and the dates, I don't know. I mean, they must have been there on or around the 12th and 13th of July, because that's when the refugees start getting moved. But it's how you did it, and on what dates these things occurred on, and what orders were given, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1039, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now briefly see P2280 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is, would you agree, a document dated the 19th of July, 1995, sent by the UNPROFOR commander to the Zagreb headquarters? And I would now like us to show page 3 of this document. Page 3, under the heading "Srebrenica." [In English] "General Smith asked General Mladic for an account of the activities of the BSA troops in the aftermath of the fall of Srebrenica. General Mladic was at pains to point out that Srebrenica was finished in a correct way. He stated that the population who moved to Potocari were evacuated at their own request and with the full co-operation and help of UNPROFOR." [Interpretation] Do you recall this conversation with Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, let us now go back to the first time that the Serb Army entered the built-up area of the enclave, the Srebrenica town itself. Had UNPROFOR evacuated all civilians from the Potocari part of the town and that that was in keeping with the wish of the Bosnian Government, that the enclave should not be defended, but, rather, that they should try to break out of the area, whereas the civilians should be evacuated, as reported by the ambassador, and is it true -- or let me put it more precisely. Is it true that we did not actually find any civilians there because they had already been evacuated before we entered?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evacuation from Potocari did not -- it occurred sometime after the Bosnian Serb Army had entered the built-up area of the enclave. It isn't a -- those were separated by days, those two events. But from what you have shown me, the -- and on my own -- on the evidence of the events, the defence of the enclave collapsed, and they withdrew out of the enclave, I believe, in the direction of Tuzla in the majority of cases. The UN then set about, after that, evacuating the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, did you receive any information or any evidence to the effect that somebody -- or some people wanted to leave Srebrenica, but were not allowed to by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what point? When they were all clustered around Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were gathered in Potocari before the Serbs entered. Now, once the Serbs entered, once they did that, was there anyone who wanted to return to Srebrenica from Potocari rather than go on to Tuzla? Do you have any information to that effect, that there were people who wanted to remain in Srebrenica, as Mladic said -- or, rather, do you have information to the effect that the Serbs had prevented someone from returning or anyone from returning to Srebrenica? And, of course, I'm referring to civilians here.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that everybody -- the civilians all 'round and in Potocari got on the buses and left as refugees. I don't recall an account of anybody wanting to return to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please see D144 quickly. Let us now see what the treatment was of the other neighbouring protected area, Zepa. Here we have before us a document dated the 23rd February 1995, whereas it should be 1996. Obviously, this is a typo. And it says that this is an analytical summary of the reasons for the fall of Srebrenica and Zepa. Now, knowing that Zepa fell in July 1995, this must be a mistake. Now, we'll see if there's any other date there. Now, we see this is a cover letter, and the Military Security Service Administration, Jusuf Jasarevic, is sending an analysis to Army General Rasim Delic, describing how the fall of Zepa and Srebrenica came about. Could we now see the fifth page of this document, please. 6, page 6, please, of the document itself. Here, where it begins with: "At a time --" Page 6 in e-court, please. We had the page just a moment ago before us. So that's page 6 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, it's a long time ago that I read the indictment. Is Zepa included in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I would note, however, that -- not in the sense the Court is asking about it. I don't know exactly where the accused is going with this, but, of course, I note there was reference to Zepa in this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 5 in e-court. Mr. Tieger is absolutely correct. All I'm trying to show here is to see what the pattern of conduct towards the civilians was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in paragraph 3 from the top, where it says: "At the time of the Chetnik attack on Zepa on 9 July 1995, about 6.500 people lived in this area. They and the members of the 285th Light Brigade were well supplied with all types of foodstuffs." And then a few sentences on, it says: "After the commander of this UNPROFOR battalion crossed over to the command of the Chetnik forces, the new Ukrainian Battalion commander handed over all the weapons at his disposal to our soldiers. These were immediately used to defend Zepa. And according to several displaced persons from Zepa, he even sent false reports to UNPROFOR Command in Sarajevo, saying that members of the Ukrainian Battalion had been directly attacked and requesting NATO air-strikes against the Chetniks." [Interpretation] Do you recall, General, that your command was informed that they had been attacked, and here we can see that it was -- that that was information was false?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I recall is that at some point, a date I can't recall, but at this time in this month, the Ukrainian Detachment - it wasn't a whole battalion - in Zepa had all its weapons and armoured vehicles taken off it by the defenders. The exact circumstances as to the occurrence of that, I never got -- none of those things, I never got to the bottom of. I don't understand the sentence about "the commander of this UNPROFOR battalion crossed over to the command of the Chetnik forces, the new Ukrainian Battalion commander." I don't recognise that event at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, one of -- well, actually, the official commander felt that he was in danger, and he actually crossed over to the Serbs. And then this following -- the subsequent person, he reported as he did. But this is not the only case of this nature. There were other instances where it was reported that Muslims actually took weapons off the UNPROFOR members and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the last portion of his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- which was the case in other enclaves and on other occasions. Were there such instances?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both sides did this. The other case I can recall of the Bosnian Government doing it was in two cases. One was in Gorazde, and there's another later on in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us now take a look at Gorazde. Can I have 1D985, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it to come up -- 1D985, yes, now we have it. General, let me tell you that there was the possibility that a renegade Serb would capture a vehicle, but here we see that this was something that was committed by an entire unit, and I'm referring to the confiscation or seizure of your weapons. My question relates to what you said a little earlier, where you mention that both parties did this. Yesterday, we saw that Serbs had prohibited any kind of illegal conduct, and here we see that an entire unit actually confiscated weapons from you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't confiscate it. They had their weapons confiscated. Yes, that's what I was referring to in the Gorazde case. To expand on my remarks: That isn't true that it was a rogue Serb soldier doing these things. After the hostage-taking in May, there was a number of weapons and armoured vehicles taken and never given back by the Bosnian Serb Army. And I can personally recall seeing at least one of those at Zepa in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that at the time when there were hostilities between us and you, General? Was that at the point where we declared that you were the enemy, or was this done just out of the blue, the same way that it was done in Gorazde and Bihac?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the incidents were different, but the result was the same, that UN weapons and equipment were taken by one side or the other and used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, General, we seized weapons from you and captured your troops at the moment when you started attacking us, whereas the Muslims were doing this at the time while you were protecting them; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, the incidents are different, yes. They -- in this case, the one on the screen, the Bosnians take the Ukrainian company commander, in particular, hostage while they steal the weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We've all seen this document. I would like to tender it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I wondered where the questioning was going. And it did veer for a moment into something that seemed relevant, which was the actions of the Bosnian Serb forces vis-a-vis the UN, but I'm hard-pressed to see what the relevance is of this document and the questions pertaining to what the Muslim forces did with respect to UN and UN equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you help us in this regard, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, easily. Because we expected this, our restrictions on the supplies of war material by UNPROFOR into protected areas -- or, rather, we were very wary of such supplies because we knew that one day they would fall into the hands of the Muslim army. We didn't do this because we were evil, but for military reasons, and this example clearly illustrates that. And the other reason is to show the pattern of conduct by the Muslim side toward those -- toward their protectors, UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But how is that relevant to your case? In any event, we'll admit that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1040, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, with all due respect, it is relevant because our concern regarding the supplies provided by UNPROFOR to the enclaves --
